newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak court rejects govt referendum motion.
newsitem.headline: Slovak court rejects govt referendum motion.

text.p: Slovakia's Constitutional Court on Wednesday rejected a government motion seeking a ruling on whether a referendum on the direct election of the president was legal.

"The government motion has been rejected because the government is not legally charged to carry out the referendum," court spokeswoman Marianna Mochnacova told Reuters from the court's headquarters in Kosice, eastern Slovakia.
The court's refusal to rule opened the way for the referendum, called by outgoing President Michal Kovac following an opposition-sponsored petition, to go ahead.

"The government cannot be a party to the argument for a ruling (on the constitution)," the court said. "The petitioner is not a participant of the argument before the court and can therefore not propose any motion."
The referendum on a direct election has been set for May 23-24 alongside another on whether or not Slovakia should apply for NATO membership.

The government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar, an avowed political foe of incumbent President Kovac, tried to get the court to declare the referendum unconstitutional in the hope of postponing or preventing it.
The referendum was seen as an attempt to prevent Meciar from assuming presidential powers when Kovac steps down at the end of his term next March.

Under the present constitution, the president requires a three-fifths parliamentary majority to be elected. But in the present parliament neither the ruling coalition nor the opposition would be able to muster the necessary majority.
Presidential powers would then pass to the prime minister pending new parliamentary elections in the autumn of 1998.

The court said the ruling stipulated the Interior Ministry and the referendum commission had the duty to ensure the referendum was carried out. The ministry has so far refused to move on the referendum pending a court decision.
